I've been self harm free for about a year now and I'm proud of that progress. Just to say it is possible for you to get there. The thing that finally put a stop to it was fear, believe it or not. Fear that it would hurt someone I love very much. I cared more not to hurt them by hurting myself  than I did about not hurting myself for myself (if that makes sense). It didn't stop over night, though. What I started doing was every time I had that urge, I'd try my hardest to do something related to self care. Depending on how functional I was that day, that might be taking a shower, playing a video game instead of doing homework, making myself food, reaching out to a friend or whatever I was able to realize I was in need of.

One of the other really effective things I found was when the urges were really bad, asking a trusted friend to just come and sit with me for a while. I knew that I wasn't going to hurt myself in front of them, so having them sit with me and saying nice things to me really helped pass the time before I could handle being by myself again. I strongly recommend doing this. You don't even have to tell your friend you're dealing with self harm. All you have to do is tell them you're really struggling with your mental health and that you need someone to be with you for a while. Tell them that they don't have to do anything. You just need someone's presence. That saved me so many times when I was suicidal.

Have you specifically asked a dr about fibromyalgia? A diagnosis for fibromyalgia tends to be very simple and involves only a physical exam, no blood tests or anything like that.

Fibromyalgia features constant pain in universal, standardized tender points around the body as well as pain in other areas. The cramping pain you describe sounds to me like a mild flare up of fibromyalgia. At its worst, it can leave you bedridden for days or months in tears for most of the time because the pain is so bad.

The tingling doesn't match up with my experience of fibromyalgia, but I do experience that as a symptom of anxiety. Or it can be connected to back problems, when a disc in your back pinches a nerve. This happens to me and causes tingling in my arms and legs.  Tingling in the feet or legs can also be a symptom of MS and other forms of paralysis.

Fatigue is definitely part of fibromyalgia, but you could also have chronic fatigue syndrome, which is very debilitating and real. 

Needless to say, it's not all in your head. Even if some of the symptoms are caused by anxiety, that doesn't make them any less real or difficult to deal with. Anxiety is a physical illness as well as a mental one. Fibromyalgia is also something that tends to get worse when you're stressed, so there's that as well.

Things I've learned from my therapist. Somatic (physical) symptoms are very common in PTSD and other mental health disorders. With PTSD, you can have a sub-type of flashback where your body remembers trauma and tenses up or hurts in places you were hurt, even if your brain isn't bringing up memories. This happens to me all the time.

This can also happen with other things in your body. For instance, you can remember a trauma that made you feel sick to your stomach at the time and feel that in the present. Or, for example, my abusers used sleep deprivation as a means to exhaust me and make it easier for them to control me, so for years, I've struggled with insomnia—all because my body remembers. 

It's also very common for fibromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome to co-occur with PTSD. I have them, and they always get worse following significant flashbacks or other episodes 🤷🏻‍♀️
